children: By Mackenzie Tatananni
Quantinuum wants to build a quantum computer by the end of the decade that solves real-world problems and that businesses can use every day — and now it has concrete plans to do just that.
On Thursday, the company unveiled a slew of upcoming changes to its Nexus platform, designed to simplify quantum application development and automate error correction.

The announcement came ahead of Quantinuum's third-quarter earnings report, which handily topped consensus views. The company reported a narrower-than-expected loss of 29 cents against analysts' calls for 37 cents. Revenue more than tripled to $9.1 million, ahead of the $8.1 million analysts had expected.

Perhaps more importantly — as major Wall Street firms continue to warm up to quantum stocks — the company hiked its full-year revenue outlook to a range of $31 million to $34 million, signaling continued commercial momentum. Management previously guided for $28 million to $32 million.

Fueling that optimism, Quantinuum noted it struck the largest cloud agreement in company history, a multi-year extension of an existing deal with a "global financial institution" that includes committed access through both Apollo and Nexus.
Shares fell 9% during Thursday's regular session as stocks broadly slid, but rebounded 2.8% to $30.60 in extended-hours trading after the report.

In practice, the overhaul to Nexus removes the need to manually calibrate physical quantum bits, or qubits, which in Quantinuum's case are individual ions levitated in a vacuum. Instead, developers can write code directly for logical qubits.

These virtual units spread information across a cluster of linked physical qubits to shield the system from environmental "noise" —  the heat, vibrations, and stray signals that typically bungle calculations.

"As we've been looking at our own roadmap for fault tolerance, we see a huge industry need to make these tools much more accessible to users than they are today," Jenni Strabley, the head of Quantinuum's compute platforms group, said in an interview with Barron's. "Giving experts the tools to be more efficient is incredibly valuable. And enterprise users — someone like a research chemist who doesn't have a lot of quantum computing experience — are a key target audience."
Nexus debuted two years ago as a cloud workflow and user management tool. It has since evolved to support requirements for next-generation quantum machines, particularly application development.
Nexus marks the next step following Quantinuum's late-2025 launch of Guppy, a quantum programming language CEO Rajeeb Hazra called a "paradigm shift."
Building on that momentum, the company released Guppy FT this September to help developers write, compile, and execute fault-tolerant quantum programs.

Unlike classical computers that encode information in ones and zeros, different quantum modalities harness atomic ions, tiny electrical circuits, and particles of light, which are inherently more sensitive to changes in their environment.

Efficacy in a controlled laboratory setting won't necessarily translate to the real world. In turn, attention has shifted toward error correction. Errors will always inevitably occur to some degree, just as they do in classical machines, but the goal is to detect and suppress faults before they derail operations.

The overhaul to the Nexus platform will introduce new capabilities with each successive generation of hardware through Apollo, the error-corrected system Quantinuum plans to release in 2029. As the physical systems mature, so will the software, allowing developers to turn their attention to components like libraries and algorithms.

It is tempting to describe the quantum landscape as a simple "race" toward more capable systems. That framing fails to capture the field's true complexity, as many players act as ecosystem enablers rather than pure competitors. IonQ and International Business Machines, for example, offer foundry services to peers, while Microsoft and Amazon provide cloud access to third-party hardware.

What's going on in error correction, however, is nothing short of a race. Demonstrating superior error-correction rates carries immense clout ahead of the late 2020s, when most players have pledged to deliver fault-tolerant systems that operate reliably in spite of hardware flaws. Even the federal government is applying pressure, aiming to deploy a "scientifically relevant" quantum computer at a national lab by 2028.

Quantinuum recently announced a landmark error-correction result, achieving just five failures per million operations — a 99.9995% fidelity rate that approaches fault-tolerant performance. This surpasses the previous benchmark set by Alphabet-owned Google in 2024, with the caveat that Google's result was demonstrated on a different type of hardware.

Morgan Stanley analysts noted that the breakthrough "solidifies Quantinuum's lead among the pure plays" while effectively closing its main technical gap with Google. Though Quantinuum had led in protected operations, Google previously held the edge in demonstrating that "more protection keeps lowering errors," analysts wrote.

The analysts were referring to distance scaling, a key threshold in fault-tolerant quantum computing where increasing the "code distance" by adding more physical qubits to a single logical qubit dramatically suppresses the logical error rate rather than amplifying it.
While Quantinuum has shown "a steeper improvement per step than Google," analysts conceded that Google's result was rigorously peer-reviewed and decoded in real time.

As Google and Quantinuum compete on the technical front, Quantinuum continues to expand its commercial footprint, whereas Google keeps most of its quantum operations in-house. Now on its third-generation system, Quantinuum plans to launch its next quantum computer, Sol, in late 2027.
